text: You get two integer arrays, preorder and inorder. They are the preorder and inorder traversals of the same binary tree. Build that tree and return its root.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — preorder is root, then left, then right. Inorder is left, then root, then right. So preorder tells me who the root is: it's always the first one. And inorder tells me how to split: everything left of the root is the left subtree, everything right of it is the right subtree. Is that right?
Are the values unique? That matters a lot. If two nodes had the same value, I couldn't tell which one in inorder is the root. And can I trust that both arrays really come from one tree?
Values are unique, and yes, the input is always valid.
Great. Are there any constraints on the input size?
There are one to three thousand nodes, and each value is between negative three thousand and three thousand.

Okay. So n is at least one — I never get an empty input. And the tree can be a straight chain, so the depth can be up to three thousand; I'll keep that in mind for recursion. Quick check on the example: preorder three, nine, twenty, fifteen, seven; inorder nine, three, fifteen, twenty, seven. Three comes first in preorder, so it's the root. In inorder, three is at index one, so nine is the left subtree and fifteen, twenty, seven is the right. Left size is one, so in preorder the next one value goes left and the rest goes right. Doing the same on each side gives three, nine, twenty, null, null, fifteen, seven. That matches.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would be to do the same split, but scan the inorder range each time to find the root. That scan is linear per node, so on a chain it adds up to n squared. It still passes at three thousand, but it's wasted work. This problem reminds me of divide and conquer on a tree: each call owns one subtree, and the root splits it into two smaller problems of the same shape. The only slow part is finding the root in inorder. Since values are unique, a hash map from value to inorder index, built once, makes each lookup constant time.

Here's the plan. One: map each value to its inorder index. Two: a helper takes pre L, where the subtree starts in preorder, plus in L to in R, its range in inorder. Three: the root is preorder at pre L, left size is its inorder index minus in L, the left child starts at pre L plus one, and the right child at pre L plus left size plus one. One thing worth flagging — those are two different coordinates. At node nine, the preorder position is one but the inorder range starts at zero, so one shared pair for both recurses forever. Left size is the only bridge between the arrays. There's a trade-off here: a global preorder index skips that math, but only works if I build left before right. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. Build tree fills the map from inorder, then calls build on the whole range, starting at preorder zero. Build returns null on an empty range, reads the root, looks up its index, computes left size, and recurses with the two ranges from the plan. One thing worth flagging — the base case checks the inorder range, in L greater than in R, not pre L. An empty range means an empty subtree, so I return null before I ever read preorder at pre L. The last leaf's empty right child arrives with pre L equal to n, so reading first would go out of bounds.

Let's dry-run the code on example one. I expect three, nine, twenty, null, null, fifteen, seven. The row that matters is the root's right child. At the root, left size is one, so the right subtree starts in preorder at zero plus one plus one, which is two — that's twenty. In inorder it covers indexes two to four, which is fifteen, twenty, seven. Both line up, and the tree comes out as expected, in eleven calls: five nodes and six null returns — exactly two n plus one. Corner cases: a single node, negative one, gives negative one — negative values are fine as map keys. Only right children, one, two in both arrays, gives one, null, two — that's where the plus one matters: without it, the right call reuses the root, then reads preorder at minus one. Only left children gives one, two.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear: building the map is linear, then there are exactly two n plus one calls to build, each doing constant work thanks to the map. Space is linear for the map, plus O of h for the recursion stack. Worst case the tree is a chain, so the recursion depth is three thousand and one, which is fine on the default stack; if n were in the millions, I'd switch to an explicit stack. And the map is worth it: on a three-thousand-node left chain, a linear scan took two point seven five milliseconds, and the map took zero point one nine five. Oh, one more thing — the map only works because the values are unique. That's why I asked about it at the start. With duplicates, the tree wouldn't even be unique.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You named left size as the bridge between the two arrays, and showed why one shared pair of bounds recurses forever. You explained the plus one in the right subtree's start with a concrete input where dropping it reads out of bounds. And you backed the hash map with real numbers, and called out that the global index version depends on building left before right. Good work.
